problem: Existing exploration/navigation methods either use rigid hand-coded rules, drift-prone metric SLAM, or learning-based systems needing large pre-training. Prior bio-inspired and active-inference navigators depend on past observations or pre-training and adapt poorly to dynamic changes or unknown areas.
motivation: Automated factories need robots that explore and navigate unknown, dynamic environments without pre-training and at low compute. Active Inference frames mapping, localisation and planning as one predictive belief-updating process, which could give an interpretable, online, zero-shot navigator.
key_idea: An Active Inference agent builds an online topological cognitive map with hypothetical predicted nodes and selects actions by minimising Expected Free Energy (with MCTS), on a modular ROS2 stack, so it explores and reaches goals without pre-training.
insight: Planning on believed odometry, with Dirichlet-updated transition probabilities, keeps exploration working after drift and after undetected or moved obstacles (drift demo in a home run; box-moved demo). Human interventions in the table are lower than baselines in the small warehouse and the big warehouse, but not clearly better than Gbplanner or Frontiers in the home. The evidence is small-scale and largely qualitative; goal reaching is near-optimal only within the ~14 m imagination horizon.
method: Topological cognitive map: nodes are states defined by believed pose and observation; a POMDP generative model with B_s, B_p, A_o, A_p matrices, and B_p a growing tensor of poses added as new locations are found, with a user-set influence radius.

Map expansion: accessible areas from LiDAR range are added as hypothetical nodes with unknown observation; place recognition uses a stitched 360° panorama compared to memory by an SSIM threshold; a confidence threshold decides between updating A_o and relocalising.

Decision making: discrete yaw-range actions (plus optional STAY); actions chosen by a softmax over Expected Free Energy (information gain + preference/utility), with MCTS to limit prediction cost; the exploration/exploitation weight is configurable.

Dynamic obstacle handling: Dirichlet pseudo-count updates of transition matrices B with positive or negative learning rates (7/-7 forward experienced, 5/-5 predicted, smaller for reverse) so blocked transitions lose probability and new states are created.

ROS2 architecture: four modules (model, odometry, sensor processing, motion control); the model uses believed odometry over sensor odometry; motion is by Nav2 or potential field; modules are replaceable; tested on Turtlebot3 and ROSbot XL.
Goal reaching: goals given as positions or RGB observations; exploration term set to 0 and goal preference weight 5, with imagination up to about 14 m.

setting.backbone: Active Inference generative model (POMDP with Expected Free Energy + MCTS), online-updated; SSIM-based place recognition; Nav2/potential field for control
setting.observation: 2D 360° LiDAR (12 m) + single camera / stitched 360° panorama
setting.action_space: discrete yaw-orientation ranges (e.g. 30° bins, 8 ranges) + optional STAY, executed by Nav2 / potential-field controller
setting.simulator: Gazebo (Amazon warehouse mini/small/large, 156 m² home) plus a small real maze

numbers_note: No standard benchmark metrics; results are given in figures (coverage vs distance, distance comparison) and a human-intervention count table (Table 2). The intervention counts are: ours 0/1/0/2 vs Gbplanner 2/4/2/2 vs Frontiers 3/2/0/5 vs FAEL 3/2/5/5 (mini/small/big/home).
results: On the 280 m² warehouse (5 runs), the agent covers the area in roughly 100 m of travel, comparable to Gbplanner and better than Frontiers, while using fewer sensors than Gbplanner. It needs fewer human interventions than Gbplanner, Frontiers and FAEL in most environments (0/1/0/2 across mini/small/big/home), and it copes with drift and moved obstacles. Goal reaching follows near-optimal paths within a ~14 m horizon.
limitations: Small-scale evaluation (5 runs, mostly simulation, tiny 5 m² real maze); no standard benchmarks or formal quantitative metrics beyond figures and intervention counts.
Goal reaching degrades beyond the ~14 m imagination horizon, where the agent briefly explores before replanning.
Computational cost on robot platforms not formally shown; perception and place recognition (SSIM panoramas, LiDAR-based accessibility) are simple.
builds_on: Active-inference topological cognitive map (de Tinguy et al. ours_model)
